notes: Attorney General reference on wholesale cocaine conspiracy sentences; double jeopardy limits intervention.

enrichment.short_title: AG Reference: unduly lenient sentences in Brick Lane cocaine conspiracy
key_facts: Whiteway, Connell, Long and Nadarajah pleaded guilty to conspiracy to supply large quantities of cocaine from storage units at Truman's Brewery, Brick Lane.
Computer trading records showed turnover exceeding £7.6 million and handling of over 142 kilograms of cocaine before a 14.8 kilogram seizure on 5 September 2003.
Judge Mackinnon sentenced Whiteway to 12 years, Long to 9 years, Connell to 8 years and Nadarajah to 7 years for their respective roles.
The Attorney General referred the sentences as unduly lenient under section 36 of the 1988 Act.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 against sentences imposed at Southwark Crown Court.
enrichment.outcome: Leave to refer granted; the Court held Whiteway's sentence was unduly lenient but, applying double jeopardy, declined to increase any of the four sentences.
enrichment.ratio: Major organisers of wholesale Class A drug distribution may attract sentences somewhat lower than importers but the difference is small; where a sentence is unduly lenient double jeopardy may nonetheless preclude intervention, especially where the discount for a late guilty plea was conspicuously generous.
legal_issues: Whether sentences for a multi-million pound cocaine conspiracy were unduly lenient
Appropriate starting points for a leading wholesaler compared with importers
Effect of double jeopardy on Attorney General references
Relative culpability of principal organiser, record-keeper, courier and single-delivery facilitator
linked_authorities: Attorney General's Reference No 4 of 2002 [2003] EWCA Crim 2488
Attorney General's Reference No 4 of 2002 (Lowe) unreported 30 October 2003
Attorney General's Reference No 1 of 2002 [2003] 1 Cr App R(S) 389

notes: Second probate appeal after Italian witnesses' police statements; Ladd v Marshall satisfied and rehearing ordered.

enrichment.short_title: Couwenbergh v Valkova: probate rehearing after attestation evidence
key_facts: Carnwath J pronounced for a 24 October 1990 will leaving Mrs Adam's estate to Dr Valkova rather than her Dutch niece and former executor Mr Couwenbergh.
The Italian witnesses Di Gregorio later told police they signed in the hallway without seeing Mrs Adam sign and did not know they were attesting a will.
Legally aided Dr Valkova pursued costs exceeding £200,000 against the foreign claimant, including freezing his Dutch home.
Permission for a second appeal was granted under Taylor v Lawrence on the fresh attestation evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal with permission against a probate order admitting the Italian will, following police statements from attesting witnesses.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; order of Carnwath J set aside including the costs order; matter remitted to the Chancery Division for rehearing with trial costs reserved.
enrichment.ratio: Fresh evidence that attesting witnesses were not in the testator's presence when she signed satisfies Ladd v Marshall and probably would have affected the outcome; where fraud or perjury is alleged but not finally established, remittal for rehearing is preferable to requiring a fresh action.
legal_issues: Whether fresh police statements from attesting witnesses should be admitted
Application of Ladd v Marshall to due execution evidence
Whether a second appeal was permissible under Taylor v Lawrence
Appropriate remedy where attestation and knowledge-and-approval findings may be undermined
linked_authorities: Ladd v Marshall [1954] 3 All ER 745
Taylor v Lawrence [2002] EWCA Civ 90
Hamilton v Al Fayed [2001] EMLR 15

confidence.notes: Appellate reasoning on fresh evidence and remittal is detailed, though underlying fraud is not finally determined.

notes: Fire damage quantum appeal; saved refurbishment costs deducted and claimant's profit loss not remitted.

enrichment.short_title: Barkin v Re-Source: saved refurbishment credit on spool replacement
key_facts: Barkin Construction negligently caused a fire destroying about 130,000 fibre-optic cable spools awaiting refurbishment at Re-Source's Deeside warehouse.
Corning had to purchase over 100,000 new spools at a cost exceeding $1.28 million because no used spools were available.
The judge awarded the full replacement cost without deducting saved refurbishment charges of over $500,000.
Re-Source never traded profitably and closed its Deeside plant in December 2001 after the fibre optics market collapsed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against part of a Technology and Construction Court quantum judgment on fire damage to bailee-held spools.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; award reduced by saved refurbishment costs; no remittal on Re-Source's own loss of profit claim.
enrichment.ratio: Where destroyed chattels would have required refurbishment, Corning's loss is replacement cost less saved refurbishment expenditure; a claimant must prove actual loss of profit by reference to subsequent events and cannot recover full refurbishment revenue without showing shortage of work or increased costs.
legal_issues: Whether saved refurbishment costs should be deducted from replacement awards
Whether Re-Source proved loss of refurbishment revenue attributable to the fire
Relevance of subsequent market collapse to quantum
Whether quantum should be remitted for a differently pleaded profit claim
linked_authorities: Harbutt's Plasticine Co Ltd v Wayne Tank & Pump Co Ltd [1970] 1 QB 447

confidence.notes: Quantum principles and refusal to remit are clearly articulated on undisputed fire causation.

notes: Lightman J refused probate of alleged Jerusalem codicil as concocted after testator's death.

enrichment.short_title: Bokhari v Harb: fabricated codicil refused probate
key_facts: Emile Harb's 1988 will left most of his £1.4 million estate to accountant Mr Bokhari rather than his nephews Khalil and Samir Harb.
The defendants alleged a 1990 Jerusalem codicil executed during mourning for Suleiman Harb, but no copy was found in the testator's safe after his 2000 death.
Lawyer Mr Gheath gave contradictory accounts to an Israeli solicitor and at trial, the second version omitting family involvement.
The testator never mentioned the codicil when instructing English solicitors in 1995 and 2000.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Probate trial before Lightman J on competing claims to a 1988 will and an alleged 1990 codicil executed in Jerusalem.
enrichment.outcome: Probate of the codicil refused; Mr Phillips's appointment as executor terminated; 1988 will probate to proceed.
enrichment.ratio: Contradictory attestation evidence, absence of any post-execution reference by the testator, delayed disclosure and implausible mourning-period absences support a finding that the codicil was concocted shortly before October 2000 rather than duly executed in January 1990.
legal_issues: Whether the alleged codicil was duly executed under English law
Credibility of Mr Gheath and attesting witnesses
Whether the testator would have made a family-favouring codicil during Jerusalem mourning
Effect of contradictory pre-trial statements on probate evidence

confidence.notes: Detailed fact findings and clear refusal of probate on fabrication grounds.

notes: Mobile mast GPDO scheme; Article 6 breach by late LPA notice does not invalidate planning permission.

enrichment.short_title: Nunn v SoS: Article 6 breach but lawful T-Mobile mast permission

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (General Permitted Development) Order 1995

key_facts: T-Mobile erected a sub-15 metre mast under GPDO permitted development rights after Leeds City Council served prior-approval refusal one day late.
Dr Nunn made representations opposing siting and appearance on health and property value grounds.
An inspector upheld T-Mobile's section 174(2)(c) appeal that no planning breach occurred once the 56-day period expired.
The council conceded Article 6 was infringed by the late notification.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of an inspector's decision quashing enforcement notices against T-Mobile's mobile phone mast.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; T-Mobile's planning permission remained valid; Dr Nunn's remedy lay in damages against the local planning authority, not setting aside permission.
enrichment.ratio: The GPDO scheme is Article 6 compliant on its ordinary meaning; incompetent operation by a local authority does not render lawfully acquired deemed permission unlawful, and section 3 cannot rewrite the scheme to revoke an innocent third party's rights.
legal_issues: Whether late prior-approval refusal invalidated GPDO planning permission
Whether Article 6 required the inspector to consider merits under section 174(2)(a)
Availability of section 3 Human Rights Act reinterpretation
Appropriate remedy where Article 6 rights are breached by authority delay

Zander v Sweden (1993) 18 EHRR 175
R (Vinos) v Marks and Spencer plc [2000] EWCA Civ 203

notes: Common intention constructive trust appeal dismissed; Oxley v Hiscock does not remove communication requirement.

enrichment.short_title: Lightfoot v Lightfoot-Brown: no constructive trust after consent order
key_facts: Mr Lightfoot transferred Mitchelswood Farm to Mrs Lightfoot-Brown under a 1996 ancillary relief consent order after divorce.
He claimed later discussions and mortgage payments of £65,000 restored his 50% beneficial interest despite legal title remaining with her.
The judge found any understanding was conditional on remarriage which never occurred and that she did not know of the £41,000 capital repayment.
Mr Lightfoot had stated in a Form E that all interest in the property had been transferred.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against dismissal of a claim for a declaration of 50% beneficial ownership in the former matrimonial home.
enrichment.outcome: Application to amend grounds refused; appeal dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Oxley v Hiscock did not dispense with the requirement that a common intention to share beneficial ownership be communicated; mortgage payments after a consent order transfer do not infer a constructive trust without an agreement or understanding beyond a conditional expectation of remarriage.
legal_issues: Whether express or inferred common intention constructive trust arose after consent order transfer
Effect of mortgage contributions without the other party's knowledge
Impact of Oxley v Hiscock on Rossett categories
Whether communication of shared intention is required

Oxley v Hiscock [2004] EWCA Civ 546
Grant v Edwards [1986] Ch 638

notes: CPR 3.10 allows correction of misdrafted extension applications; Vinos distinguished.

enrichment.short_title: Steele v Mooney: CPR 3.10 remedies misdrafted claim form extension
key_facts: A clinical negligence claim form was issued three days before limitation expired but not served within four months.
Solicitors applied to extend time for particulars of claim but omitted reference to the claim form in the application and resulting orders.
Deputy District Judge Smith later rectified the orders under CPR 3.10; HHJ Rudd allowed the defendants' appeal.
The claimant needed time to obtain expert evidence because the surgeon's records arrived late.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission on whether CPR 3.10 could rectify orders extending time for service of particulars but not the claim form.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; rectification orders restored; extensions would have been granted under rule 7.6(2) if correctly drafted.
enrichment.ratio: A drafting error in an otherwise timely extension application is an error of procedure remediable under CPR 3.10; this differs from failing to apply at all, which Vinos held cannot be cured after expiry under rule 7.6(3).
legal_issues: Scope of 'error of procedure' in CPR 3.10
Distinction between misdrafted applications and absent applications under Vinos
Whether rule 7.6(3) precludes retrospective correction
Appropriate exercise of discretion where defendants were not prejudiced

Hashtroodi v Hancock [2004] EWCA Civ 652
Elmes v Hygrade Food Products Ltd [2001] EWCA Civ 121

confidence.notes: CPR interaction and Vinos distinction are authoritatively explained.

notes: Justices' clerk wrongly applied section 1D balancing test to Rule 5(2) without-notice ASBO leave.

enrichment.short_title: Manchester CC v Manchester Magistrates: without-notice interim ASBO leave
key_facts: Mrs F complained that neighbour Mr M threatened to kill her and burn her house down on 7 October 2004.
Manchester City Council applied for an interim ASBO without notice citing fear of reprisals against a vulnerable lone occupant.
Legal adviser Louise Williams refused leave, noting no actual violence and limited incidents.
She applied Owen J's section 1D balancing test rather than the Rule 5(2) necessity test for without-notice applications.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a justices' clerk's refusal of leave to apply for an interim ASBO without notice.
enrichment.outcome: Mandatory order that leave be granted under Rule 5(2); guidance given on factors for clerks considering without-notice applications.
enrichment.ratio: Rule 5(2) requires a distinct and less stringent balancing exercise from section 1D on whether an interim order is just; threats to kill and burn a home are not low-level ASBO conduct and a clerk must consider likely defendant reaction, complainant vulnerability and counterbalancing protections.
legal_issues: Correct test for leave under Rule 5(2) versus section 1D
Whether refusal was irrational given alleged threats
Relevant factors in without-notice interim ASBO applications
Adequacy of reasons given by the justices' clerk
linked_authorities: R (Kenny) v Leeds Magistrates' Court [2003] EWHC 2963 (Admin)
R (M) v Secretary of State for Constitutional Affairs [2004] EWCA Civ 312

confidence.notes: Wrong legal test and mandatory relief are clearly identified with practical guidance.

notes: Cross-undertaking damages for blocked Acorn USA share sale; contractual principles applied.

enrichment.short_title: Triodos Bank v Dobbs: cross-undertaking damages for restrained share sale
key_facts: Mr Dobbs gave a cross-undertaking restraining receivers from disposing of Acorn USA shares pending his Companies Court challenge.
Mr Russell had agreed to buy the shares for $52,500 and paid £33,501.79 into escrow on the day the undertaking was given.
Lewison J held at trial that the shares were otherwise worthless and Mr Dobbs was not entitled to the injunction.
Release of the undertaking was delayed until May 2003; Mr Russell withdrew before completion.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Inquiry as to damages under a cross-undertaking in damages after trial held Mr Dobbs was not entitled to the interlocutory restraint.
enrichment.outcome: Receivers entitled to £33,501.79 plus interest; delay in drafting release order until January 2003 did not break causation.
enrichment.ratio: Damages under a cross-undertaking are assessed on contractual principles; where an undertaking exclusively prevented the only viable sale of otherwise worthless shares, loss of the agreed price is recoverable despite subsequent purchaser withdrawal unless the claimant failed to mitigate by unreasonable delay.
legal_issues: Assessment of damages under a cross-undertaking in damages
Causation where shares were otherwise valueless
Whether receivers failed to mitigate by delay in finalising release order
Application of contractual remoteness and mitigation principles
linked_authorities: F Hoffman-La Roche & Co AG v Secretary of State for Trade and Industry [1975] AC 295
Tharros Shipping Co Ltd v H Ellinas International Ltd [1994] 1 Lloyd's Rep 577

confidence.notes: Damages inquiry findings are detailed though mitigation analysis involves some judgment.

notes: CCRC reference; kidnapping conviction quashed after prosecution witness Hutchinson discredited.

enrichment.short_title: R v Burt: kidnapping conviction quashed after witness discredited
key_facts: Gavin Burt was convicted with Collins and Keep of kidnapping and firearm offences relying on witness Michael Hutchinson.
Collins and Keep's convictions were quashed on appeal after Hutchinson made false blackmail allegations against another man.
Police investigation showed Hutchinson's later claims were false and the Crown offered no evidence at retrial.
Burt had abandoned his appeal but the CCRC referred the case back; he remained on unconditional bail.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal following Criminal Cases Review Commission reference after co-defendants' convictions were quashed and retrial abandoned.
enrichment.outcome: Convictions quashed with Crown consent; CCRC thanked for rapid attention to the case.
enrichment.ratio: Where the Crown accepts that a discredited prosecution witness cannot be treated as a witness of truth, it is unsafe to maintain convictions that depended exclusively on his evidence.
legal_issues: Safety of convictions depending on a subsequently discredited witness
Effect of co-defendants' successful appeals on a related conviction
CCRC referral procedure after abandoned appeal
Whether Hutchinson remained a witness of truth

confidence.notes: Outcome follows Crown concession; detailed reasoning is brief but facts are clear.
